Abstract  
Biological imaging, combined with molecular insights into genes and proteins, holds immense promise 
for deepening our understanding of complex cellular systems and accelerating the development of 
predictive, personalized therapies for human health. To fully realize this potential at scale—and harness 
the power of AI/ML to extract novel biological insights and therapeutic interventions—it is necessary to 
transition from siloed datasets to globally shared, rigorously annotated, and computationally ready 
image data. This demands systematic harmonization of multidimensional bioimaging data, where 
interoperable formats, and standardized context-rich annotation, quality controls, and analytical 
pipelines transform scattered observations into a coherent knowledge base ripe for computational 
mining. Only this machine-actionable aggregation can provide the substrate for AI/ML to extract 
mechanistic insights into fundamental biological mechanisms, novel diagnostic biomarkers and 
intervention targets. Enabling seamless image data sharing in the life sciences requires addressing two 
key areas. The first is outlined in an accompanying publication, Enabling Global Image Data Sharing in 
the Life Sciences, which focuses on the publicly available repositories needed to share digital array 
data 1.  
This White Paper details a comprehensive set of requirements for integrated image data and metadata 
management - from acquisition through dissemination - ensuring the contextual information necessary 
for assessing quality, interpreting scientific validity, and enabling meaningful reuse remains intrinsically 
linked to the data throughout its lifecycle. Critically, it recognizes that generating harmonized, well-
annotated publicly available corpora of FAIR bioimage data requires these datasets to be “FAIR-from-
the-start” - an objective that can only be achieved by enabling experimental scientists to manage, 
organize, and analyze their data according to community standards from the very first experiment.  
Building on recent progress made by the bioimaging field towards establishing shared practices for 
bioimaging Quality Control (QC) and metadata capture, we present actionable recommendations to 
advance these efforts through embedding researcher-friendly integrated software infrastructure directly 
into pre-publication workflows, thus transforming disorganized data capture into structured, shareable 
resources ready for aggregation and reuse. Our ultimate goal is to expand the use of streamlined tools 
and practices thus transforming how researchers capture, annotate, analyze and eventually publish 
bioimaging data thus laying the foundation for a new era of data-driven discovery. 
Background and Motivation 
Biological images provide unique temporal and spatial data about biological molecules, which 
significantly enhances our understanding of complex biological systems. Moreover, sharing the vast 
amount of information captured in biological image data promises to advance human health and the 
economy, the same way sharing of genomics data and protein structure data has (i.e., the Human 
Genome Project, https://www.genome.gov/human-genome-project; and the Protein Data Bank - PDB,  
https://www.rcsb.org). Achieving this vision will require the interoperability, integration, and sharing of 
bioimage data across laboratories and research studies, thus maximizing the value of the billions of 


 
 
2 
dollars invested annually in research around the globe. Data sharing is globally recognized as highly 
desirable 2,3, but too often, preclinical bioimaging data remains inaccessible, because standardized 
practices and consistent metadata for acquisition, analysis and publication are not yet 
employed/enforced. Moreover, even when shared, bioimaging data often lacks sufficient information to 
evaluate its validity and reproducibility, to assess its reusability, drive machine-actionable aggregation 
and ultimately provide the substrate for AI/ML to extract scientific and therapeutic advances. 4–12.  
Funding agencies have been working to improve the situation, for example, by establishing data 
governance and preservation policies 13–15 that make it mandatory for researchers to provide detailed 
data management and sharing plans 13,16–18. To improve reproducibility in research, many publishers 
now require more detailed materials and methods sections 6,19–22. In 2016, stakeholders from academia, 
industry, funding agencies, and publishing arrived at a set of FAIR Data Principles—“Findable, 
Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable”—which are expected to improve the machine-actionability of 
data thus expanding its utility well beyond its original purpose 23. Several international initiatives are 
engaged in addressing the challenges associated with the implementation of FAIR principles during 
bioimage data generation and post-acquisition processing (Supplemental Table 1). For many years, 
the Open Microscopy Environment (OME) has produced tools, metadata models and shared bioimage 
data file formats to facilitate the generation, pre-publication management, integrated analysis and post-
publication sharing of contextual-information rich image data 5,24–29. Organizations of bioimaging 
experts across academia and industry (see Supplemental Table 1) have more recently coalesced 
around improving standard practices for instrument QC and metadata 8,20,30–43 Through these multi-
stakeholder collaborations, individual laboratories and core facilities are partnering with manufacturers 
to develop shared metadata standards and conduct inter-laboratory studies validating quality control 
methods 44–50. Despite limited funding, these groups have driven progress through voluntary 
commitments, enabling tangible—if still limited—progress across the bioimaging field. While challenges 
remain, these efforts lay the foundation for generating reliable, well-documented bioimaging data that 
meets FAIR principles and are critical to unlocking the full potential of quantitative bioimage-based 
research and its biomedical applications. 
While most scientists endorse FAIR principles and intend to share bioimage data, persistent technical 
barriers hinder implementation. The first challenge involves the lack of federated public bioimage data 
repositories spanning individual institutions to the national level 1,51–53. The second stems from 
fragmented practices in metadata annotation, bioimage acquisition, analysis, and dissemination - 
where lack of locally-available and usable software platforms, inconsistent standards and poor 
machine-readability create bottlenecks in automation and prevent the generation of bioimage datasets 
that are ready to be shared. This fragmentation particularly impacts pre-publication data management, 
where the absence of integrated software platforms and unified workflows available to researchers at 
the local level, limits both immediate analysis and long-term reuse potential. Addressing these gaps 
requires user-friendly tools that not only integrate with experimental workflows, 54–56 but also bridge the 
divide between local data production and analysis, and broader research cyberinfrastructure. 


 
 
3 
Here we summarize recent progress toward standardized data and metadata practices for bioimages, 
while recommending how to extend this work to address remaining challenges. Our goal is to make 
software platforms, best practices and usable tools accessible to all biomedical researchers, regardless 
of their expertise, available resources, or geographic location. We adopt a comprehensive framework 
that follows the bioimage-data lifecycle (Figure 1). Beginning with data generation, where challenges 
include sample preparation and bioimage acquisition, we then examine issues affecting the reliability 
and reproducibility of post-acquisition processing, visualization, and quantitative analysis. Finally, we 
address the critical importance of data management and stewardship in maintaining robust links 
between bioimage data and metadata throughout the entire research process and often culminating in 
publication. Building integrated software platforms that ensure complete provenance tracking and 
quality assessment, forms the essential foundation for achieving truly FAIR-compliant microscopy data. 
Only through such comprehensive approaches can we maximize the scientific value of bioimage data, 
both for its original research purpose and for enabling new discoveries through data sharing and reuse. 
Challenges and Recent Progress Associated with Data Generation 
The preservation of data and metadata starting from data generation lies at the very heart of the 
bioimage data lifecycle, involves considerations made at the planning phase of the research project, is 
relevant before the sample hits the bioimage acquisition platform, informs all subsequent bioimage 
processing steps and is essential to ensuring the scientific value of shared bioimage data. 
Good practices in data generation and management that are deployed throughout the entire data life-
cycle and ensure that data are “FAIR from the start” are essential for rigorous and reproducible 
quantitative bioimage-based biomedical research and for producing bioimage data that can be 
interpreted, trusted, and reused through model-based and data-driven mining, aggregation, reanalysis, 
and integrative modeling. It is crucial that third-party data users have ready access not only to the 
bioimages themselves, but crucially to machine-actionable representations of all data-related 
information (i.e., “bioimage metadata”) that allows to evaluate the suitability of given datasets for 
answering specific scientific questions before accessing or downloading them. This “bioimage 
metadata” comprises two types of metadata31: (i) data provenance metadata, which describes the 
experimental conditions, sample description and preparation, bioimage acquisition (i.e., hardware 
description and bioimage acquisition settings), and bioimage processing, visualization, and analysis; 
and (ii) QC metadata, which describes system performance recorded through standardized QC 
protocols and metrics. 
Advances in Capturing Experimental Conditions and Sample Preparation Metadata 
Accurate interpretation of microscopy data requires comprehensive documentation of the entire 
experimental workflow. This includes: (1) all pre-imaging procedures, (2) biological sample origin and 
preparation methods, (3) labelling protocols and reagents, (4) mounting techniques, and (5) 
characteristics of specimen holders during bioimaging. While traditionally reported in Methods sections 
4,19,20,50,57, this information must now be captured and retained with the bioimage, as structured, 


 
 
4 
machine-readable metadata to enable data reuse. The bioimaging field is making significant strides 
toward standardization. The REMBI framework33, developed through multi-stakeholder consensus, 
establishes core metadata categories for light, electron, and X-ray microscopy to ensure data 
interpretability and reusability. Along the same lines, minimum information guidelines for 3D 
microscopy, highly multiplexed tissue images and cell migration experiments have recently been 
developed to guide the documentation of experimental procedures and sample preparation 58–62 
Effective implementation requires three key components: standardized ontologies for consistent 
knowledge representation 63–67, automated metadata capture tools 32,62,68–73, and seamless integration 
with data management platforms. Together, these elements create the foundation for FAIR-compliant 
microscopy research25,74. 
Advances in Capturing Microscopy Acquisition Provenance and QC Metadata  
Quality assessment, reproducibility, interpretation, and reuse of bioimage data depend on detailed 
information about hardware specifications, bioimage acquisition settings, and instrument performance 
at the time of data acquisition 30,31. A comprehensive technical description of the bioimaging system 
configuration enables calculation of key parameters such as spatiotemporal resolution, system noise, 
and the physical and temporal dimensions of pixel data. An instrument performance assessment plan, 
including regular tracking of standardized QC metrics, quantifies performance changes over time 44–47. 
These QC metrics compare expected (theoretical) values with observed (empirical) measurements and 
with baseline values recorded at instrument installation (time zero). Importantly, QC metrics also 
support characterization and calibration of derived bioimage analysis outputs, such as co-registration 
measurements. Capturing the overall state 32 and performance of the microscope as metadata at the 
time of acquisition is essential to identify potential batch effects in large datasets 9. Such batch effects 
can significantly impact the performance of artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms, 
making it critical to document instrument state and performance for accurate result interpretation 9,10. 
Ensuring the Validity and Reproducibility of Image Data Visualization, and Analysis 
A detailed workflow must be provided to independently assess the quality, reproducibility, and 
interpretation of bioimage data analysis, as outlined in recent community guidelines 19,75,76. Analysis 
metadata should also include data size, computing hardware specifications, and networking 
requirements. This is essential, as data analysis pipelines typically involve complex dependency chains 
of multiple software packages (e.g., open source software tools such as FiJi, QUPath and napari, etc.; 
commercial tools such as Imaris, Huigyens, etc.) that must be precisely described to ensure 
reproducibility. Consequently, the metadata associated with the analysis  phase, must specify the exact 
versions of all software components to prevent discrepancies caused by subsequent software updates. 
Manually reporting all dependencies beyond the primary software is impractical and is best managed 
using automated package managers (e.g., the pip freeze command). 
Since image processing pipelines often involve multiple tools, it is essential to store intermediate and 
final results, along with associated metadata, in a harmonized and comparable format across different 


 
 
5 
software tools 77. To address this, developers have made significant progress in using containerization 
technologies 78–81 and workflow management tools 82–87. Future efforts should focus on enhancing the 
robustness of these solutions and encouraging their widespread dissemination and adoption. 
If an analysis environment is recreated using the same hardware, operating system, bioimage analysis 
software, and parameter settings, analyzing the same dataset at different locations should yield the 
same results. However, in the case of algorithms that rely on randomness, results within an acceptable 
margin of error are considered sufficiently similar 88–90. In addition such cases require sharing additional 
details such as random seed values and other relevant software parameters.  For instance, in deep 
learning, reproducing results from a retrained or new model necessitates access to both the code and 
model weights, which should be shared in interoperable formats like the Open Neural Network 
Exchange (ONNX).   
Everyday Stewardship of Bioimage Data and Metadata During Active Data Production 
Data stewardship is an intrinsic and essential aspect of generating high-quality bioimage data that is 
“FAIR from the start.” For this to happen, data stewardship must involve the entire lifecycle of the data, 
starting with the planning phase and continuing during experimental design and execution, sample 
preparation, data acquisition, post-processing, visualization, and analysis. In addition, data stewardship 
must outlive the research project to ensure that well-documented published data remains available for 
re-use, as detailed in the companion manuscript 91. Specifically, correct data stewardship ensures that 
the conditions used to generate, process, analyze, and validate data are transparent, documented, 
propagated alongside the data and automatically reported to downstream users in both human-
readable forms (i.e., scientific publications) 4,20,21,57 and structured machine-readable metadata 
frameworks 
92–94. Cloud-ready data exchange formats 
28,29,42 and standardized Application 
Programming Interfaces (APIs) are necessary for integration of bioimages and results 28–30,32,33,58,95. 
This, in turn, ensures that data can be trusted, correctly interpreted, reproduced, and reused through 
data aggregation, mining, integrative modeling, and further analysis (including AI/ML). Proper data 
stewardship is crucial from the start, to avoid wasting time and resources later trying to re-generate 
data that has been lost or cannot be interpreted, and consequently, promote efficiency and 
sustainability (economic, environmental, and societal) 96,97. 
As such, effective data stewardship requires well-maintained, enterprise-grade, scalable, open-source, 
and democratized Research Data Management and Sharing (RDMS) cyberinfrastructure, capable of 
providing the necessary pipelines to move data along from generation to analysis and sharing 51 (Figure 
1). This cyberinfrastructure should include the following; 1) Persistent Identifiers (PIDs) for research 
resources, individuals, publications and data 98–101; 2) shared file formats and associated APIs 28,29,102; 
3) the use of community-defined ontologies 103,104105,106; 3) bioimage metadata specifications 30,33,58; 
and 4) community defined Next Generation Metadata frameworks 95. This cyberinfrastructure should 
interface with Electronic Lab Notebooks (ELN) and Laboratory Information Management Systems 
(LIMS) and, whenever possible, automatically capture and propagate output metadata from all relevant 


 
 
6 
instrumentation (including but not limited to robotic, microfluidics, and bioimage acquisition hardware) 
107,108. In summary, cyberinfrastructure should cover the following three interconnected aspects: 
○ WHAT information should be captured in Bioimage Metadata: develop community standards 
models for all aspects of image metadata 30,31,33,58. 
○ WHERE Bioimage Metadata should be stored: develop community specifications and shared 
APIs (i.e., OME-NGFF and Next Generation Metadata)28,29,95,109 to ensure data and metadata are 
stored in synch with each other across the bioimaging data flow. 
○ HOW Bioimage Metadata should be captured: develop easy to use tools to facilitate metadata 
annotation, data curation, and seamless integration of all aspects of the bioimaging pipeline (i.e., 
integration with LIMS, ELNs, and hardware instrumentation; ontology-enriched, REMBI-based, 
modular template spreadsheets; ad hoc graphical interfaces to collect microscopy metadata) 
32,69,71,72,110–114. 
FAIR quality control in Recently Emerging Bioimaging Modalities  
A set of recently developed bioimaging modalities are emerging as techniques of choice to  quantify 
the spatial distribution of molecules and supramolecular structures at the subcellular, cellular, tissue, 
and organismal levels as reviewed in 115–117118–120. These techniques include spatial RNA profiling 
methods capable of resolving hundreds of probes at subcellular resolution using light microscopy, in 
situ sequencing (ISS), and capture assay. In addition, several highly multiplexed antibody-based 
bioimaging techniques have also been developed and commercialized. Cryogenic transmission 
electron microscopy (cryo-EM) provides images of biological matter in a frozen-hydrated, near-native 
state. The cryo-EM field is recognized as a good example of effectively annotating metadata and 
stewardship of raw and derived data 33. The cryo-EM community agrees that detailed metadata must 
be made publicly available alongside the data and that metadata standards must be reviewed regularly 
to ensure fitness and relevance to the evolving community needs 33,121. Data sharing of cryo-EM derived 
122–124) and raw data 125,126 - both with associated metadata - has already been established and is 
enforced by most publishers,  
We advocate for a similar approach to be adopted for multiplexed RNA, protein, and multi-omic 
bioimaging datasets. The recent introduction of these methods, combined with their complexity and 
diversity, resulted in various workflows related to sample processing, reagent QC, bioimage acquisition, 
bioimage processing, and bioimage analysis without agreed-upon community standards 127. The 
establishment and wide adoption of such standards are essential for cross-lab and cross-platform data 
interoperability and analysis, which is even more critical to the community since these data are 
expensive to acquire 116,118,128 and are associated with a number of consortia efforts 129–131. Critical 
details related to sample preparation, reagent validation, and platform-specific bioimaging parameters 
must be recorded and shared using community-defined metadata. We highlight specific challenges 
around harmonizing multiplexed image processing and reporting that limit current ability towards FAIR 
data 23.

Recommendations Toward Global Bioimage Data Generation and Stewardship 
Standards 
All stakeholders have a role to play in implementing these practices. Funding agencies should support 
the development of tools, protocols, and metadata standards by bioimaging communities to ensure 
their routine adoption by core facilities and users. Manufacturers can facilitate automated access to 
comprehensive, community-defined technical descriptions of instruments and quality control (QC) 
metrics within the metadata they provide with the bioimage data 107,108. Publishers ought to require that 
microscopy metadata—including hardware specifications, bioimage acquisition settings, and QC 
metrics—be included as part of data submissions. Investigators should embrace best practices 
established by the bioimaging research community, providing both human- and machine-readable 
metadata to ensure their data meet FAIR principles. Finally, fostering the creation, dissemination and 
support of resources in multiple languages is essential for universal adoption of these standards. 
In Text Box 1, we outline recommended steps to promote the generation and stewardship of image 
data that is “FAIR from the start,” ready for sharing and reuse. Additional details are available in 
Supplemental Material.

Data Generation Recommendations 
Overcoming challenges related to the generation of bioimage data that is “FAIR from the start” requires 
specific solutions that should be planned for and carried out by all interested stakeholders. To guide 
the development of these solutions, we provide the following specific recommendations: 
● Promote the widespread adoption of Persistent IDentifiers (PIDs) to enable the FAIR 
description of all scientific entities, to facilitate reporting and reproducibility and to recognize the 
essential roles of bioimaging scientists and core facilities in the research enterprise 98–101. This 
recommendation is backed by recent cost-benefit analyses 99,100 that revealed significant financial 
advantages associated with the adoption of PIDs which would be related to reductions in staff 
salaries, the time saved from tedious data entry, and in the facilitation of technology advances. 
Example of commonly used PIDs include:  
o Research Organization Registry (ROR) 133,134 for institutions and free standing core facilities.  
o Research Resource Identifier (RRID) 134,135 for rsearch core facilities that are part of larger 
institutions, reagents, research resources and instruments. 
o Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for datasets, publications and other digital resources. 
o Open Researcher and Contributor ID (ORCID) 136,137 for individuals. 
o PIDINST for instrument instances 101,138,139. 
 
● Promote the collection of full technical descriptions of microscope hardware specifications, 
image acquisition settings, and QC protocols and metrics (aka Microscopy Metadata) that 
comply 4DN-BINA-OME (NBO-Q) microscopy metadata specifications 30,31 which is being 
developed by consensus by bioimaging scientists and instrument manufacturers 107,108. Technical 
descriptions captured in Microscopy Metadata must become obligatory aspects of the production of 
any image data; in their absence, image data cannot reliably be quantified, reproduced, or reused 
and ultimately loses scientific value even when it is shared. As such, Microscopy Metadata should 
be made transparently available to microscope users, automatically collected using community tools 
32,71,72,140, and encoded using shared metadata frameworks 28,29.   
● Ensure that instrument maintenance and quality assessment are adequately supported to 
ensure that they become common practice at all core facilities and individual laboratories utilizing 
microscopes and regardless of local resource availability. Specific funding mechanisms should be 
considered to provide the necessary instrumentation, training and personnel or traveling metrology 
services for under-resourced areas. This will allow for the performance of instruments to be 
evaluated at regular intervals using community-defined metrology standards and QC procedures 
that are appropriate for each experimental question 44–46. Additional metrics might need to be 
collected for specific types of experimental approaches and desired outcomes.

● Emphasize large infrastructure investments in core facilities and regional infrastructural 
hubs 97 who employ trained personnel, including bioimaging scientists, data stewards, image 
analysts, and research software engineers. Such shared infrastructure would increase efficiency 
and reduce costs by maintaining and assessing the performance of instruments; promote the 
dissemination of technological advances (hardware and software); facilitate user training; provide 
guidance for experimental procedures, image analysis, and data stewardship; and provide image 
analysis and Research Data Management and Sharing (RDMS) services to facilitate the deposition 
of FAIR data packages containing the appropriate image metadata to specialized bioimage 
repositories. These infrastructure investments should include providing legal support to review data, 
identify appropriate Creative Commons (CC) and Open-Source Software (OSS) licensing, and/or 
carry out Personal Information (PI) redaction (human subject data).  
● Invest in the development of open-hardware devices (e.g., robotic devices, fluidics systems, 
environmental control devices, microscopes, etc.) to carry out all aspects of data generation as the 
most appropriate way to democratize advanced technology and to ensure the efficient use of 
resources. 
Data Processing and Analysis Metadata Recommendations 
Once acquired, bioimages often require complex processing, visualization, and analysis to extract 
quantitative information about signal intensity, as well as the location, morphology, association, and 
movement of biological entities. To ensure that bioimage processing and analysis results are 
reproducible and FAIR-ready, community-defined guidelines should be followed. In particular: 
● Image processing and analysis workflows should be shared as binary containers (e.g., Docker, 
Singularity, or Podman) that include the complete software environment, ensuring identical 
pipeline execution for all users. 
● The workflow should specify which aspects of microscopy acquisition (e.g., magnification, 
resolution, signal intensity) may influence processing and should be encoded in the metadata 
accordingly. 
● Every component of the processing and analysis pipeline—including data structure and size, 
rendering and processing steps, algorithm versions and input parameters, and computing and 
networking requirements—must be documented in both human- and machine-readable formats 
to guarantee interpretability, reproducibility, and downstream reuse. This metadata should reside 
either within the image data file (such as image rendering and processing information) or in the 
workflow documentation (such as algorithm versions and parameters). 
● Therefore, it is essential to capture analysis metadata using community-defined specifications 
and storage frameworks. This approach maximizes efficiency in extracting and tracking 
information across all pipeline stages without requiring repeated time-consuming access to the 
image data itself.

Data Stewardship Recommendations 
● Responsible stewardship of data and associated metadata throughout the entire lifecycle of 
quantitative bioimaging experiments is essential to ensure rigor, reproducibility, and the 
production of high-quality bioimage data that are interpretable and ready for reuse in accordance 
with FAIR principles. 
● Generating and stewarding FAIR image data requires full transparency, management, and 
reporting of all information related to data generation (including experimental conditions, sample 
preparation, and image acquisition) as well as processing and analysis (such as image analysis 
and visualization). 
● RDMS cyberinfrastructure that supports the generation and pre-publication stewardship of high-
quality FAIR image data should be accessible to all biomedical researchers using microscopes, 
serving as a crucial prerequisite for bioimage data sharing and reuse. 
● This bioimaging RDMS cyberinfrastructure must include advanced computing resources and 
data repositories that integrate data stewardship, metadata annotation, visualization 
environments, processing pipelines, and analysis routines (including AI/ML), all connected 
through high-speed networks to facilitate efficient data transfer. 
● Such RDMS cyberinfrastructure is best supported by user-friendly, enterprise-grade, robust, and 
continuously maintained open-source software that covers all steps of the bioimaging pipeline—
from experimental management (e.g., LIMS or ELN), through image acquisition (e.g., Micro-
Manager, Pycro-Manager, Python Microscope), to processing, visualization, analysis, and data 
workflows (e.g., CellProfiler, Fiji, napari, CellPose). 
● When proprietary software and instruments are necessary, community-defined standards must 
be applied to ensure transparency of all relevant algorithms, input parameters, and instrument 
configurations and performance. 
● Metadata collection and reporting must follow community-defined standards at two closely 
connected levels: 
○ Human-readable, primarily documented in Materials and Methods 4,20,21,57, representing 
a subset of Bioimage Metadata that allows users to understand and describe the 
bioimaging experiment. 
○ Machine-readable, fully captured in Bioimage Metadata, which includes all information 
needed to trace the lineage (provenance) and quality of bioimage data, ensuring 
comprehensive quality, reproducibility, and reusability 28,29,95 . 
● To ensure Machine Readability:  
○ Metadata should be encoded in community-specified frameworks to be associated with 
standardized bioimage data file formats 28,29,95, or workflow documentation, and equipped with 
readily available software API to facilitate the transfer of information across the different steps

of the bioimaging pipeline. For example, it should be possible to be put in an SQL database 
automatically.  A potential framework that could fulfill these requirements is LinkML92,141. It 
allows for easy authoring of metadata schemas in the YAML format, which can be exported into 
other formats. It is also able to create classes in various programming languages that can serve 
to validate metadata.  
○ It is imperative to use specific annotation tools and automation at all aspects of the 
bioimaging pipeline to ensure that image processing, visualization, and analysis pipelines can 
leverage metadata. Particular emphasis should be given to (i) automated processes for 
microscope systems and peripheral components, including community-defined QC procedures 
to ensure optimal instrument performance 30,58; (ii) automated metadata annotation at all phases 
of the image-data life cycle 32,71,72; and (iii) integrated image processing, visualization, and 
analysis pipelines. 
○ Metadata annotations should be backed by ontologies and knowledge graphs. Ontologies 
provide descriptions of the hierarchical relationship between concepts and can be used to make 
metadata machine-readable. Their role in the harmonization of knowledge and data in 
biomedicine is increasingly recognized, especially in the context of AI, where they can provide 
valuable constraints that make ML more efficient 104. Tools such as the Ontology Look Up 
Service (OLS) 103 can be used to locate appropriate ontological terms, although further 
development is needed to help sort through duplicates and identify which terms should be used 
in different contexts.  
● Quality, transparency, reproducibility, and reusability require standards defined by all bioimaging 
community stakeholders. 
○ Recent advancements have made it clear that the community, when participating in bioimaging 
organizations, networks, and initiatives, is willing and ready to take on this challenge. 
○ However, deliberate, direct, and targeted funding is needed to ensure that ongoing 
standardization efforts can be expanded to cover all essential aspects of the bioimaging 
pipeline. 
● In addition to being essential for generating standards, community organizations are ideal ways to 
promote the broader dissemination and adoption of standards via education, training, and outreach. 
As such, novel funding models should be implemented to ensure the sustainability of these essential 
endeavors, promoting the reuse and advancement of quantitative bioimaging and science as a 
whole. 
● Cyber infrastructure for RDMS will impact the economy beyond the biological research enterprise. 
Tested and trusted microscope QC protocols, and commonly accepted and unambiguous reporting 
criteria will be beneficial to the many applications of quantitative bioimaging for cellular analysis, 
including pathology, cell therapies, and regenerative medicine.

Abstract: Biological imaging, combined with molecular insights into genes and proteins, holds immense promise for deepening our understanding of complex cellular systems and accelerating the development of predictive, personalized therapies for human health. To fully realize this potential at scale—and harness the power of AI/ML to extract novel biological insights and therapeutic interventions—it is necessary to transition from siloed datasets to globally shared, rigorously annotated, and computationally ready image data. This demands systematic harmonization of multidimensional bioimaging data, where interoperable formats, and standardized context-rich annotation, quality controls, and analytical pipelines transform scattered observations into a coherent knowledge base ripe for computational mining. Only this machine-actionable aggregation can provide the substrate for AI/ML to extract mechanistic insights into fundamental biological mechanisms, novel diagnostic biomarkers and intervention targets. Enabling seamless image data sharing in the life sciences requires addressing two key areas. The first is outlined in an accompanying publication, Enabling Global Image Data Sharing in the Life Sciences, which focuses on the publicly available repositories needed to share digital array data 1. This White Paper details a comprehensive set of requirements for integrated image data and metadata management - from acquisition through dissemination - ensuring the contextual information necessary for assessing quality, interpreting scientific validity, and enabling meaningful reuse remains intrinsically linked to the data throughout its lifecycle. Critically, it recognizes that generating harmonized, well- annotated publicly available corpora of FAIR bioimage data requires these datasets to be “FAIR-from- the-start” - an objective that can only be achieved by enabling experimental scientists to manage, organize, and analyze their data according to community standards from the very first experiment. Building on recent progress made by the bioimaging field towards establishing shared practices for bioimaging Quality Control (QC) and metadata capture, we present actionable recommendations to advance these efforts through embedding researcher-friendly integrated software infrastructure directly into pre-publication workflows, thus transforming disorganized data capture into structured, shareable resources ready for aggregation and reuse. Our ultimate goal is to expand the use of streamlined tools and practices thus transforming how researchers capture, annotate, analyze and eventually publish bioimaging data thus laying the foundation for a new era of data-driven discovery. Background and Motivation Biological images provide unique temporal and spatial data about biological molecules, which significantly enhances our understanding of complex biological systems. Moreover, sharing the vast amount of information captured in biological image data promises to advance human health and the economy, the same way sharing of genomics data and protein structure data has (i.e., the Human Genome Project, https://www.genome.gov/human-genome-project; and the Protein Data Bank - PDB, https://www.rcsb.org). Achieving this vision will require the interoperability, integration, and sharing of bioimage data across laboratories and research studies, thus maximizing the value of the billions of 2 dollars invested annually in research around the globe. Data sharing is globally recognized as highly desirable 2,3, but too often, preclinical bioimaging data remains inaccessible, because standardized practices and consistent metadata for acquisition, analysis and publication are not yet employed/enforced. Moreover, even when shared, bioimaging data often lacks sufficient information to evaluate its validity and reproducibility, to assess its reusability, drive machine-actionable aggregation and ultimately provide the substrate for AI/ML to extract scientific and therapeutic advances. 4–12. Funding agencies have been working to improve the situation, for example, by establishing data governance and preservation policies 13–15 that make it mandatory for researchers to provide detailed data management and sharing plans 13,16–18. To improve reproducibility in research, many publishers now require more detailed materials and methods sections 6,19–22. In 2016, stakeholders from academia, industry, funding agencies, and publishing arrived at a set of FAIR Data Principles—“Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable”—which are expected to improve the machine-actionability of data thus expanding its utility well beyond its original purpose 23. Several international initiatives are engaged in addressing the challenges associated with the implementation of FAIR principles during bioimage data generation and post-acquisition processing (Supplemental Table 1).
